context: a letter from T. W. Woodbury, which you are answering
exchanges:
I am exceedingly obliged to you for favouring me with specimens of bees and their comb from Africa. I suppose the bees are apis Adansonii as they appear to tally with the description of that species in the Naturalist’s Library. They appear almost identical with apis Ligustica with the exception of being smaller. Very careful comparison of their comb with that of mellifica enables me to pronounce the cells exactly the same ⁠⟨⁠size⁠⟩⁠

How singular it appears that this small bee as well as the large species apis testacea do not vary one iota in the size of their cells from our European species! It would be very interesting to ascertain if the small species so common in India (apis Indica) also makes the same sized cell.

These bees being so small would not repay the trouble of attempting to import them, but I still have a strong impression that the large Indian species (apis dorsata) would be very valuable. ⁠⟨⁠I⁠⟩⁠ dare say you may have seen my queries regarding them together with the answers in “The Field.” Little practical information has resulted, nor do I yet see my way to taking any steps for their importation. Have you noticed that the first four hives of Ligustica sent by me to Australia have all got there in safety?

I have never heard if the piece of partially completed artificial comb proved at all interesting to you

Yours greatly obliged | T W Woodbury

C. Darwin Esq

I thought & still think that I wrote to thank you for the artificial comb, which interested me much; but if you did not get a letter, it must have been lost or I did not write it.—

With apologies, Dear Sir, | & my best thanks, | Yours very faithfully, | C. Darwin
